advances: An exact comparison cover for any given positive anchored circuit; it does not assert that the moved cover masses equal the moved actual depths.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
Each old body contains an interior ball, and by support functions a smaller concentric ball remains in every nearby version of the same body. There is also a uniform outer radius by local Hausdorff continuity. If two such bodies have Hausdorff distance $\epsilon$ and share a ball of radius $r$ centered at $a$, then each is contained in the other dilated by $1+\epsilon/r$ about $a$: adding $\epsilon B_d$ is bounded by adding $(\epsilon/r)(K-a)$. Hence their symmetric-difference volume is $O(\epsilon)$, by the uniform volume bound and the volume of the two outer dilations. The cap mass is therefore locally Lipschitz in $p$ at every fixed threshold, uniformly in that threshold.

For nearby $b_1<b_2$, the cap-mass difference is the sum of slab volumes over the finite base set. On the anchor, a fixed ball about $y$ stays in the body, and the thresholds considered run through a fixed central subinterval of this ball. Its section areas have a uniform positive lower bound, including counting measure in dimension one. All slice areas on every fiber have a uniform upper bound from boundedness. Thus for positive uniform constants $c,C$,

$c(b_2-b_1)\le F_j(p,b_1)-F_j(p,b_2)\le C(b_2-b_1).$

Fubini justifies these bounds; the endpoint level sets are null for $d$-dimensional volume. Take two thresholds on opposite sides of $b_j$. By continuity they bracket all sufficiently nearby $\tau$ for every nearby $p$. This gives the unique local quantile, and the two slope bounds give its monotonicity and bi-Lipschitz estimates in $\tau$. The lower slope and the uniform bound on variation of $F_j$ in $p$ also give the joint Lipschitz estimate by comparing the inverse equations.

The weighted sum of quantiles has the same strict decrease, with a uniform positive lower decrease rate. At the old mass its value is $\sum_j\rho_j b_j=A\cdot z$, because the caps pass through the mark and the continuous normals balance. The same bracketing and slope argument gives the unique Lipschitz root. At any point $(z,x)$ the weighted sum of the shifted margins is now exactly zero, so some margin is nonnegative. This proves the whole-plane cover by closed caps. The cap containing a given point gives the claimed bound on that point's depth; division by the positive total mass proves the normalized assertion.

statement:
Let $P\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty finite set and $K_w(p)\subset\mathbb R^d$, $w\in P$, be compact convex bodies depending locally Hausdorff-Lipschitz on a finite-dimensional parameter $p$ near $p_0$. Write $\mu_p=\sum_{w\in P}\delta_w\otimes(\mathcal L^d|_{K_w(p)})$ and $M(p)=\sum_w|K_w(p)|$. Use a finite list of closed caps

$H_j(b)=\{(w,x):v_j\cdot w+u_j\cdot x\ge b\},\qquad |u_j|=1.$

At the old family suppose each $H_j(b_j)$ passes through the same mark $(z,y)$ with $z\in P$, $y\in\operatorname{int}K_z(p_0)$, and has the same raw mass $\tau_0$. Suppose $\rho_j>0$, $\sum_j\rho_j=1$ and $\sum_j\rho_j u_j=0$, and set $A=\sum_j\rho_j v_j$.

Each function $F_j(p,b)=\mu_p(H_j(b))$ has a unique local inverse in the threshold, $Q_j(p,\tau)$, for $(p,\tau)$ near $(p_0,\tau_0)$. It is locally Lipschitz jointly and locally uniformly decreasing and bi-Lipschitz in $\tau$. There is a unique nearby locally Lipschitz mass $\tau_c(p)$ with

$\sum_j\rho_j Q_j(p,\tau_c(p))=A\cdot z.$

The shifted closed caps at these thresholds all have raw mass $\tau_c(p)$ and cover the whole plane $\{z\}\times\mathbb R^d$. In particular the new restricted maximal normalized depth over $z$ is at most $\tau_c(p)/M(p)$.
title: Anchored cap quantiles and exact circuit covers
